title: Analytical data dictionary
text:
This dictionary documents the record grains and principal fields used in the recruitment reanalysis, longitudinal detection pilot, and retained cross-sectional foundation. It describes derived analytical data; record-level FIA observations are intentionally not distributed with the public repository.
The v2.0 detection analysis is now an exploratory pilot. The revised research direction is implemented in the recruitment report. Record-level recruitment data and predictions remain local; aggregate results and audits are exported.

title: Analytical data dictionary
text:
Recruitment endpoint and linked fates

A conservative new live maple sapling tally has SPCD=318, STATUSCD=1, 1 <= DIA < 5 inches, RECONCILECD=1, and no PREV_TRE_CN. It must occur on comparable sampled area. This is not individual seedling survival, an exact recruitment date, or a count of stems that entered and died between visits.
Baseline saplings are followed using successor PREV_TRE_CN to baseline TREE.CN, restricted to the expected successor plot. Retain fate status, reconciliation code, diameter, species corrections, and condition continuity. Unlinked or out-of-sample records are not deaths; living stems reaching 5 inches have left the sapling size class, not disappeared biologically.
One fully sampled current-pair follow-up has no live TREE rows and missing derived sapling metrics. The audit reconciles its absence using source records; the new endpoint builder handles this verified zero explicitly. This is not authorization to fill all missing tree measurements with zeros.
Historical feasibility removes the single-evaluation restriction but retains baseline northern-hardwood and established-maple eligibility. Its 2,308 intervals are provisional and reuse physical plots. Protocol and observation comparability must be validated before treating them as an analysis cohort.

data/processed/recruitment_condition_pairs.rds retains all 932 source pairs, including excluded observations, at condition-interval grain. data/processed/recruitment_sapling_fates.rds retains 1,593 tagged baseline stems at stem-interval grain. Neither file is distributed.

0 / 1 / NA
At least one qualifying new live maple sapling at follow-up, defined only on eligible intervals.

Baseline maple SEEDLING.TREECOUNT summed by condition, checked against calculated counts; above-five microplot counts may be estimated.

Baseline live maple sapling TPA_UNADJ divided by microplot condition coverage; not a statewide survey weight.

Whether every relevant subplot has a direct predecessor link; all false in this snapshot because the source field is empty.

logical

logical

0 / 1 / NA

The endpoint definitions and protocol audit expose the rules.
Recruitment models use log1p count, log1p maple sapling stem density, log1p established-maple basal area, microplot coverage, and interval. Each model uses only its declared subset. Scaling is fit within training data; the full-refit bootstrap repeats scaling. See the analysis contract.

Survey-priority outputs
The recruitment-survey-*.csv tables report aggregate strategies on the existing model populations. They do not contain individual site recommendations.

Meaning

Fixed illustrative fraction and floor(n * fraction) condition-interval count. Not an actual survey budget.

Expected target count under uniform allocation within cutoff-score ties. Can be fractional.

Expected targets divided by capacity; different from the fraction of all targets captured.

Expected targets divided by all target conditions in the evaluated population.

Distinct plots selected using stable source-key order, showing why condition capacity is not equal field cost.

Full-refit county-bootstrap percentile limits for selected target fraction or its paired difference, as identified by the output table.



RI availability tables have a different purpose: screen indicates record presence only. LENGTH_CLASS_CD, seedling-source codes, and RI sampling-status codes remain raw codes in that preliminary export. Their subsequent decoding and sampling checks are in the separate RI measurement audit below.


RI measurement outputs
The recruitment-ri-*.csv tables describe the checked baseline measurement subset, not fitted predictions. Record-level data are held in the ignored data/processed/recruitment_ri_audit.rds bundle.







Field
Meaning




baseline_ri_frame_valid
Complete code-1 forest-condition RI microplot coverage, valid subplot linkage, and agreement with the condition’s sampled proportion.


baseline_ri_available
Frame and record checks plus the May-September plot-date plausibility screen. Missing RI measurements remain unavailable.


ri_class_1 through ri_class_6
Maple tally counts in the six verified length classes; unavailable outside the accepted baseline frame.


ri_all_count
Total recorded maple RI count across length classes and permitted source groups. Not independent seedlings or genets.

Sum of classes 3-6, at least one foot long; compared with ordinary hardwood counts on identical units.


ri_tall_count
Sum of classes 5-6, at least five feet long; not the one-inch DBH sapling boundary.

No qualifying RI maple tally on a verified available baseline frame; not no germination or no future recruitment.

Baseline year 2016-2018 has an inspected annual supplement; the 2016 archived copy is a draft. Not universal protocol certification.

Descriptive recorded-entry fraction and county-bootstrap limits for the declared group, not prediction accuracy or a causal effect.



Nine intervals have valid RI maple tally zeros; 832 lack baseline RI and retain missing length information. Ten ordinary-zero intervals contain RI maple only below one foot. These observation states are deliberately distinct.


Analytical units
The primary analytical unit is one baseline–follow-up forest-condition pair. Each visit retains the composite key PLT_CN + CONDID. Tree and seedling records are first aggregated independently to visit-condition grain and only then joined to pair records, preventing many-to-many row inflation.

Live trees have STATUSCD = 1. Sugar maple is resolved from REF_SPECIES as Acer saccharum, FIA species code 318. For tree (i), the plot-basis basal-area contribution is

Field
Unit
Definition

ft²/acre
Sum of frame-corrected live-tree contributions: microplot records divide by micrprop_unadj, subplot records by subpprop_unadj, and applicable macroplot records by macrprop_unadj.

ft²/acre
Sugar-maple component of the frame-corrected live-tree density.

ft²/acre
Frame-corrected basal area of live sugar-maple TREE records with DBH 1–4.9 inches.

logical
TRUE when at least one live sugar-maple TREE record has DBH 1–4.9 inches. The longitudinal model uses its baseline value.

ft²/acre
Frame-corrected basal area of all live TREE records with DBH ≥ 5 inches.

The derived total is checked against FIA COND.BALIVE; the pipeline enforces strict correlation and absolute-error gates that detect use of a wrong sampling frame. Implementation: R/basal_area.R.

Longitudinal model transformations
The model-complete loss cohort contains 677 baseline detections, including 75 loss events. Continuous predictors are standardized after log1p transformation where stated. Cross-validation relearns every center and scale from its training counties only.







Model field
Source and transformation

baseline logical indicator, with FALSE as the reference

The primary loss fit is a binomial GLM with county-cluster CR1 confidence intervals. Five-fold internal validation holds out whole counties. A county random-intercept GLMM is reported only as sensitivity evidence. Implementation: R/longitudinal_models.R.
The secondary appearance cohort contains 255 baseline non-detections, including 59 later detections. It reuses maple_sapling_present, z_established_maple_ba, z_microplot_coverage, and z_interval_years; no baseline seedling-density term is possible because all starting tallies are zero. Its four-slope model uses county-cluster CR1 intervals and the same training-only scaling and county-held-out validation protocol. Implementation: R/longitudinal_appearance_models.R.

text:
Retained cross-sectional model transformations
Continuous predictors are standardized after defining the final model-complete cohort, so one standardized unit refers to the fitted 1,072-condition primary cohort. Basal-area predictors are transformed with log(1 + x) before standardization. The scaling means, standard deviations, transformations, and cohort size are published as a separate audit table.







Model field
Source and transformation




z_maple_ba
standardized log(1 + established_maple_ba_ft2_ac) in the primary model; retained as a linear term after functional-form comparison


maple_sapling_present
factor with FALSE as the reference level


z_nonmaple_ba
standardized log(1 + nonmaple_ba_ft2_ac)


z_microplot_coverage
standardized micrprop_unadj


treated
factor with FALSE as the reference level


z_stand_age
standardized stand_age


disturbed
factor with FALSE as the reference level


z_mean_temp
standardized mean_annual_temp_c


z_precip
standardized mean_annual_precip_mm


z_year
standardized measyear



The supported release model is a mixed-effects logistic regression with a county random intercept. It separates established-tree basal area from sugar-maple sapling presence and reports adjusted probability profiles by sapling state. Ten-fold internal grouped validation holds out whole counties, relearns transformations within each training fold, and predicts held-out counties with fixed effects only. Conventional coefficient inference is supplemented by Benjamini–Hochberg adjusted p-values and a county-cluster CR1 sensitivity analysis. Model construction and support gates are in R/models.R.
The contextual full-cohort baseline uses standardized log(1 + maple_ba_ft2_ac) with a three-degree-of-freedom natural spline. It is not the primary inferential model because the exposure combines saplings and established trees.

title: Analytical data dictionary
text:
Length-study planning fields
The study design and make length-plan create planning outputs, not another fitted model. length_study_opportunity_metadata.rds is local and ignored; published recruitment-length-*.csv files are aggregates.







Field or quantity
Definition and boundary




baseline_condition_visits
Distinct baseline plot-record/condition pairs in the RI metadata screen; not validated recruitment intervals.


physical_plots
Distinct state/unit/county/plot combinations; one plot may have several historical visits.


standard_maple_record_present
At least one positive ordinary maple seedling row at baseline; a presence screen, not full count/frame validation.


successor_count
Number of distinct successor PLOT records declaring this baseline as predecessor; zero/ambiguous successors remain separate.


in_current_recruitment_plot_set
Membership in the current 903-plot cohort; nonmembership does not establish untouched evaluation data.


Q = H/N
Fraction of reconciled standard-size maple seedlings in RI classes 5-6. Undefined for N = 0; not a fraction surviving to saplings.


Paired Brier gain
Count loss minus length loss, averaged within plot then across plots. Positive favors length; differs from condition-average weighting.


loss_difference_sd
Hypothetical SD of plot-level paired losses in the planning table, not an estimated RI-model quantity.


variance_inflation
Assumed multiplier of mean-loss variance relative to independent plots; not a measured county design effect.


complete_evaluation_plots
Rounded normal-approximation precision requirement under specified assumptions; not training size, power, or calibration adequacy.


candidate_plots_at_assumed_retention
Complete-plot requirement divided by assumed retention and rounded upward; an expected-yield scaling, not guaranteed enrollment.


independent_event_units
Plug-in Wilson-width calculation at assumed fixed-rule recall; event units rather than total plots and not paired-policy precision.

title: Analytical data dictionary
text:
Interpretation boundaries

TPA_UNADJ expands records within the plot design; it is not a statewide survey weight.
Zeros are assigned only when the relevant sampling opportunity is demonstrated.
Exact FIA plot locations are confidential. Public FIADB coordinates may be approximate; this analysis neither uses nor infers them, relying only on county identifiers.
Gap flags and fitted associations are exploratory and are not causal or design-based prevalence estimates.
The retained cross-sectional size-class associations do not estimate transitions; the v2.0 repeated-condition outcome does not track individual seedlings.
Detection appearance is an operational gain state, not verified recruitment, colonization, or recovery; its weak validation does not support site-level gain targeting.
County Wilson intervals are unweighted binomial reference intervals. They ignore FIA survey design and within-county clustering and are descriptive rather than inferential county estimates.

See Analysis decisions for the complete decision log.

Local data feasibility
The Michigan snapshot contains PLOT_REGEN, SUBPLOT_REGEN, and SEEDLING_REGEN, including recorded length classes and seedling-source codes. Presence of a row is not the same as a verified sampled opportunity. Within the 922 recruitment-eligible intervals, the initial record-presence screen gives:

Only 71 of the 90 intervals also have standard baseline seedling detections. Standard and RI definitions cannot be substituted for one another, and an absent maple RI row must not become a zero without a valid frame. These counts come from the availability audit, not from a completed height-class cohort or independent test sample.
The subsequent measurement audit goes beyond that record screen: all 90 baseline intervals pass the implemented RI frame, record, and May-September date checks. They cover 311 microplot-condition intervals; all ordinary counts match the RI counts at least one foot long. Nine verified RI maple tally zeros remain zeros; ten additional ordinary-zero conditions contain RI seedlings only below one foot. Four follow-up RI frame/date flags leave 86 both-visit intervals without changing the baseline predictor cohort. Individual 2012-2015 annual supplements remain an access gap.
The 14-event overlap does not establish adequate support for a multi-height prediction model. Selecting only this subset changes the population, and all of its outcomes were already part of the explored Michigan cohort. It is not external validation simply because the extra predictors were unused earlier.

title: Survey validation plan
section: Completed measurement milestone and remaining limits
text:
Completed measurement milestone and remaining limits
The local audit has produced an eligibility flow, code/measurement reconciliation, and descriptive support tables. The checklist below records its required components; historical annual-guide coverage remains qualified, and it does not authorize a new model:

Resolve historical RI length-class and source-code definitions from the applicable guides. Standard hardwood minimum length and FIA sapling DBH boundaries are not interchangeable with RI height classes.
Verify REGEN_MICR_STATUS_CD, older subplot-status fields, condition coverage, dates, and sampled microplots at the baseline used for recruitment prediction. Missing status and absent species records require explicit rules.
Reconcile total RI counts, length classes, vegetative-origin categories, and ordinary seedling tallies without forcing agreement across different minimum-size definitions. Do not include the browse-impact score as an independent cause without checking whether regeneration scarcity enters it.
Publish an eligibility flow and event/plot support. Use the same conditions for simple-count and height-information comparisons; do not compare metrics from different populations as if only the predictor changed.
Assess precision and model complexity before fitting. If the audited subset remains too weak for the proposed comparison, report the descriptive measurement audit and stop. Do not fill the gap with an optimistic model.

The descriptive result is 13 recruit-bearing conditions among 44 with baseline maple at least five feet long, versus one among 46 without. A later-year split would have ten development events and four assessment events. That does not support a strong claim about incremental forecasting value. The next study must evaluate length information against ordinary counts on a better-supported, separate sample, with a meaningful target and gain specified before evaluation.
Height information is a grounded candidate: the regional FIA study by Harris, Woodall, and D’Amato (2022) found better recruitment models with height classes than with ordinary combined counts. That precedent motivates the measurement comparison; it does not prove the Michigan subset is adequate or that a field survey would be cost-effective.

title: Survey validation plan
text:
Requirements for an operational study
The count-versus-length design now specifies the research comparison and executable precision scenarios. Its historical Michigan metadata census finds 88 positive-seedling opportunities on 79 plots before full eligibility checks, only six plots outside the current recruitment cohort. These are not new event counts or an independent evaluation set. The user has authorized a Wisconsin/Minnesota feasibility screen, not fitting on those rows. Archive access currently blocks that screen; see the access review. The conditional next-visit research target remains distinct from the operational requirements below.
Before describing a ranking as a survey tool, the following must be specified with the intended decision owner. These choices are not supplied by the current database analysis.







Requirement
Why it matters




Management or research question
Locating low advancement, locating successful recruits, estimating prevalence, and learning mechanisms require different sampling strategies.


Independently assessed target
No recorded entry is not automatically a stocking deficit, survey need, or treatable problem. Specify the field criterion and horizon without using the prediction to define the answer.


Unit of action
A management stand or physical visit is not a FIA condition interval. Define eligibility and cost at the actual sampling unit.


Measurements and timing
Specify repeatable size/height, vigor, stocking, and damage observations and the forecasting date. Use a planned horizon rather than a realized future interval.


Cost and error consequences
Travel, access, measurement time, missed problem sites, and unnecessary visits determine whether an incremental gain matters. There is no universal 25% budget.


Separate evaluation sample
Reserve locations, inventory periods, or a prospective sample before choosing models and cutoffs. Shared plots must not cross development and evaluation.



Accuracy metrics alone do not establish value. Decision-analytic methods relate predictions to meaningful error consequences; a threshold chosen solely to make a model look good is not such a preference. Vickers and Elkin (2006) provide the general methodological rationale, not forestry utilities or a recommended decision threshold for this project.

title: Survey validation plan
text:
Evaluation design
Keep low raw count and count per sampled coverage as fixed comparators. Declare which direction is useful for the independent target. If height data are evaluated, add only the scientifically motivated, supportable representation selected before observing evaluation outcomes; tune within development data.
Measure the target on a probability-based evaluation sample or a design with known selection probabilities. Assessing only model-selected sites cannot reveal missed sites or provide an unbiased model-versus-simple-rule comparison. Retain a random or stratified component across score levels, and document nonresponse and inaccessible sites. Exact FIA locations are not inferred.
Compare selected-target yield, missed-target fraction, calibration where probabilities are relevant, and actual cost per useful finding at matched plot/stand-level capacity. Use clustered uncertainty appropriate to the new sample and analyze predefined target subgroups. Report ties and protocol changes. A held-out later inventory on a known plot is a different assessment from transfer to a new location.
Choose sample size through a precision/power assessment for the paired gain that would change the decision, using realistic target frequency and within-site dependence. Do not claim adequacy from a fixed events-per-variable rule. The current 14 RI-overlap events are a feasibility warning, not a sample-size plan.

title: Survey validation plan
text:
Decision gates
Proceed to a field-facing tool only if the measurement audit passes, a real decision is specified, and the separate evaluation shows a useful improvement over the simple benchmark after accounting for collection cost and uncertainty. Failure to demonstrate an improvement is an informative result; retain the simple strategy or conclude that the target needs better measurement.
The separate scope decision now authorizes Wisconsin/Minnesota inventory acquisition and feasibility screening. It does not authorize field coordination, fieldwork, or further geography changes. The baseline measurement audit is complete with the stated historical-access qualification. The 14-event subset should not be promoted into a larger fitted model or a management claim.

title: Survey validation plan

Reproducibility
Run make survey-audit after the recruitment model bundle exists. Script 16 reproduces the capacity comparison and full-refit uncertainty; script 17 reproduces the RI availability screen. The separate make ri-audit target reproduces the measurement and support audit. The survey contract and source note separate the declared choices, local results, and external evidence.

title: Count-versus-length study design
text:
This is an optional follow-on design. The Michigan ordinary-count and linked-fate core study is complete in the revised paper. Determine whether the length distribution of established sugar-maple seedlings improves predictions of recorded sapling entry beyond ordinary seedling counts on the same sampled area. text:
Timing and the claim being tested
The primary estimand is a retrospective next-visit probability comparison conditional on the realized interval within 4.5-8.5 years. Realized T is shared by both models, so the comparison can test added length information after adjusting for observation duration. However, the actual next-visit date is not known at baseline. This estimand is not an operational forecast made at baseline.
A future forecast must instead specify a genuinely planned horizon and collect or identify outcomes at that horizon. Merely setting T = 7 when scoring existing variable-duration outcomes does not validate seven-year risks. There is no observed exact crossing date from which to reconstruct an exact seven-year recruitment event. The current study should retain the narrower conditional claim until suitable timing evidence exists.

title: Count-versus-length study design
text:
Evaluation and meaningful improvement
The primary metric is paired Brier gain: count-model squared probability error minus length-model squared error. Average the condition-level differences within each physical plot, then average across plots:
\[
D_j = \frac{1}{m_j}\sum_{i=1}^{m_j}
\left[(y_{ij}-p_{0,ij})^2-(y_{ij}-p_{1,ij})^2\right],
\qquad \Delta = \frac{1}{J}\sum_{j=1}^{J}D_j.
\]
Positive gain favors length. Equal plot weighting prevents plots with more conditions from automatically dominating the evaluation. It differs from the earlier condition-average results, which must not be substituted as the new benchmark. This is a selected-cohort comparison, not a statewide design-weighted estimate of forest condition.
Evaluate the frozen models once on the reserved sample. Resample whole counties for paired uncertainty, retaining all selected plot/condition records within each county. Such evaluation intervals are conditional on the frozen training fits; they do not include every source of model-development uncertainty. Report geographic event support, calibration curves/intercept/slope, and discrimination alongside Brier gain. With too few independent county clusters, a nominal bootstrap interval is not a sufficient precision guarantee.
A lower confidence limit above zero supports a statistical improvement for these models and this target. To claim a meaningful improvement, first declare a minimum gain delta and require the lower limit to exceed it. An interval spanning zero is inconclusive, not proof of equivalence. Neither an arbitrary Brier threshold nor a small P value supplies field utility. The necessary measurement costs and error consequences remain unspecified.

title: Ordinary seedling counts and recorded sugar maple sapling recruitment in Michigan northern hardwoods
text:
Abstract
We examined whether ordinary Forest Inventory and Analysis (FIA) seedling counts predict recorded sugar-maple (Acer saccharum) sapling recruitment in Michigan northern hardwoods and whether existing maple size structure improves prediction. The cohort contained 922 intervals on 903 physical plots across 66 counties, with baseline visits in 2011–2018 and follow-ups in 2018–2025; 169 new live saplings occurred in 100 conditions. We compared four prespecified logistic models using county-level cross-validation and 300 county-bootstrap resamples per population with model refitting. After accounting for sampled coverage and elapsed time, count-model AUC was 0.796 overall and 0.699 among 672 conditions with baseline seedlings. Counts improved Brier score relative to observation design alone, although the improvement among conditions with seedlings was uncertain. Adding maple sapling density and established-maple basal area changed Brier score by -0.00163 (95% interval -0.00529 to 0.00263) overall; the corresponding interval among conditions with seedlings also crossed zero. Separately, 1,580 comparable tagged saplings included 334 recorded deaths, 1,188 live saplings, and 58 live stems reaching 12.7 cm diameter. Seedling counts were informative about recorded entry, but the additional value of maple size structure was uncertain. These retrospective, unweighted comparisons do not establish regeneration adequacy or justify an operational management rule.

title: Ordinary seedling counts and recorded sugar maple sapling recruitment in Michigan northern hardwoods
text:
Study implications
Seedling counts were associated with new sugar-maple saplings recorded at the next inventory, but abundant seedlings do not establish successful replacement of canopy trees. In this Michigan sample, adding the abundance of existing maple saplings and larger maples did not clearly improve prediction over counts alone. Managers should distinguish recorded sapling entry from adequate regeneration and retain simple benchmarks when evaluating more elaborate indicators. The study does not identify a treatment, diagnose deer damage, or validate a rule for allocating field visits.

title: Ordinary seedling counts and recorded sugar maple sapling recruitment in Michigan northern hardwoods
text:
Introduction
Successful regeneration requires seedlings to advance into larger size classes. Michigan field studies describe plentiful small seedlings alongside limited larger regeneration (Henry et al. 2021). Sugar-maple age structure in managed northern hardwoods also shows that small-diameter stems may be old; existing saplings do not necessarily represent recent establishment (Henry and Walters 2023). These studies differ from standard FIA in their stand samples and size definitions, so their estimates cannot be treated as statewide rates for the cohort examined here.
Previous FIA research has examined the relationship between seedling measurements and subsequent recruitment. Harris and colleagues compared one seedling class with six height classes using boosted regression trees, including conspecific sapling abundance and tree basal area as candidate predictors. Their species-specific analyses were restricted to subplots with baseline seedlings, and taller seedlings were particularly informative (Harris et al. 2022). Their work provides a basis for evaluating the contribution of both seedling measurements and existing conspecific size classes. Recent northeastern studies distinguish small-seedling composition from established sapling abundance (Harris et al. 2026b) and examine recovery after disturbance over longer intervals (Harris et al. 2026a).
We examine how much information routinely available seedling counts provide about recorded sapling entry after accounting for sampled coverage and the time between inventories. We then test whether existing maple saplings and larger trees improve prediction on the same observations. This regional comparison complements earlier FIA studies while distinguishing recruitment from changes in the status of previously tagged saplings. Differences in subplot populations, seedling definitions, and validation procedures prevent direct comparison with published AUC values from studies using regeneration indicator (RI) measurements.
The primary objectives were to quantify the predictive contribution of ordinary seedling counts, assess the additional contribution of maple sapling density and established-maple basal area, and describe the subsequent fates of tagged baseline saplings. We also evaluated fixed survey-selection strategies and examined the comparability of ordinary counts with RI length measurements. These secondary analyses address possible applications and measurement extensions of the main study.

title: Ordinary seedling counts and recorded sugar maple sapling recruitment in Michigan northern hardwoods
text:
Methods

Source and cohort
The study uses the pinned Michigan FIADB SQLite snapshot and current-evaluation cohort, EVALID 262501, rather than all historical intervals. Baseline ecological eligibility is accessible northern hardwood forest (type group 800) with live established sugar maple at least five inches diameter. The selected baseline forest-type codes are 801, 802, 805, and 809. Follow-up forest type need not remain in group 800. The source pair construction requires an intended plot predecessor, one-to-one condition mapping, at least 90% mapped-area overlap relative to both visits, and a 4.5–8.5-year interval. Selection and joins are documented in the analysis decisions.
The recruitment audit additionally verifies sampled forest and mapped microplot-condition area at both visits. Both visits use the national design, the same offset microplot arrangement, and manual versions at least 5.1. Follow-ups are remeasurements; production QA codes 1 and 7 are retained. QA 7 is a supervised production check, not an invalid duplicate (Burrill et al. 2025).
Direct subplot predecessor identifiers (PREV_SBP_CN) are entirely unpopulated in this snapshot. Continuity is reconstructed from the verified plot predecessor, subplot number, and microplot condition-change matrix. Nine source pairs fail the conservative matrix-versus-condition proportion check; one contains unresolved newly recorded saplings. These ten pairs are excluded rather than assigned zero outcomes. One separately verified sampled follow-up has no live TREE records and BALIVE=0; its missing derived tree metrics are reconciled to zero only in the new recruitment dataset.
The starting current-evaluation dataset contains 932 condition intervals. The nine inconsistent mappings and one ambiguous-entry interval are distinct exclusions, leaving 922. The 914 exact-overlap intervals and the 672 intervals with baseline seedlings are alternative subsets of that retained cohort, not additional sequential exclusions. Conditions represent mapped forest domains within a plot; a physical plot can therefore contribute more than one condition. The analytical unit is one condition observed across its two linked visits, not a seedling, individual microplot, or independent stand.
Eligible rows must have complete, finite outcomes and predictor fields. The modeling code stops on missing required values rather than silently dropping different rows for different models. No predictor imputation is used. Absent species tallies become zero only after sampled-forest eligibility and record checks; an unsampled or ambiguous interval is not assigned a zero.


Recorded recruitment endpoint
The binary response is at least one new live sugar-maple sapling at follow-up: SPCD=318, STATUSCD=1, diameter at least one and less than five inches (2.54 to less than 12.7 cm), RECONCILECD=1, and no predecessor TREE record. Candidates must occur on a comparable shared sampled microplot. Reconcile code 1 can also describe entry on formerly nonforest land, so it is insufficient without the preceding sampling-frame checks (Burrill et al. 2025).
These are recorded surviving entrants into the FIA sapling class, not individual baseline seedlings followed through time. Entrants that die before remeasurement or exceed the restricted size class are not counted. Large newly recorded subplot trees are excluded because sampled area increases at the five-inch boundary. Exact mapped-area overlap is a sensitivity analysis; mapped fractions do not establish an individual stem’s lineage or exact location.


Predictors and fixed comparisons
All eligible pairs and the subset with baseline seedlings detected are principal analysis populations, fitted separately. The second asks whether measurements distinguish entrants among conditions already containing seedlings. Both use four fixed logistic models:

Training-sample prevalence only.
Observation design: baseline microplot coverage and realized interval.
Count and design: those variables plus log1p ordinary maple seedling count.
Stages and design: the count model plus log1p baseline maple sapling density and log1p established-maple basal area.

Ordinary counts sum SEEDLING.TREECOUNT and are checked against TREECOUNT_CALC. Sapling density uses FIA stem expansion and sampled microplot area; established-maple basal area uses live stems at least five inches diameter and the corresponding sampled area. Coverage is a model covariate, not a claim that raw counts were collected over identical footprints. Standard hardwood tallies omit the smallest seedlings, and counts above five may be estimated (U.S. Forest Service 2023). A recorded count is not necessarily an exact number of independent seed-origin individuals.
Training-only standardization precedes fitting. The objective is summed binomial negative log likelihood plus \(\lambda\sum_j\beta_j^2/2\) for slopes, with \(\lambda=1\) and an unpenalized intercept. This fixed ridge penalty was not tuned to optimize the findings. Ordinary GLM coefficient p-values are not attached to penalized fits. No additional competitor, beech, climate, or treatment predictor is selected after examining these recruitment results.

For each predictor, transformation precedes centering and division by its training-sample standard deviation. The same training center and scale are then applied to held-out observations. A constant training predictor uses a scale of one, preventing division by zero. The model is \(p_i=1/(1+\exp(-\eta_i))\), where \(\eta_i=\beta_0+\sum_j\beta_j z_{ij}\) and the included standardized predictors follow the four-model sequence. Coverage and interval enter as estimated slopes, not offsets. The response is binary entry, so the model does not estimate the number of new saplings or an annual recruitment rate.
The production optimizer uses Newton steps with a backtracking line search, a maximum of 100 iterations, and finite-coefficient and gradient checks. Model dimensions are zero, two, three, and five slopes, respectively, plus the intercept. Coefficients from subsequent fits to each complete analysis population are descriptive summaries; all performance claims use held-out predictions, not those full-population fitted values. The appendix reports the coefficients without unpenalized standard errors or significance stars.


Validation and uncertainty
Five folds hold out entire counties, balancing condition counts without using outcomes in assignment. All models within a population use identical observations and folds. Every physical plot stays in one fold. Scaling and fitting use training counties only. County separation prevents the same county from entering both sets, but does not impose a distance buffer between nearby plots in neighboring counties or guarantee environmental separation.
Brier score and log loss evaluate probabilities; AUC and average precision (AP) evaluate discrimination. Losses average equally over condition intervals: they are neither plot-balanced nor FIA survey-weighted population estimates. Calibration intercept and slope are estimated jointly by regressing outcomes on held-out log odds. They are diagnostics, not recalibration of predictions; the joint intercept is not a separately fitted calibration-in-the-large intercept. Mean predicted probability and the observed-to-expected ratio are also exported. Rank metrics for the prevalence benchmark are omitted because differences in fold-specific prevalence do not constitute a meaningful individual ranking.
Specifically, the Brier score is the mean squared probability error, \(n^{-1}\sum_i(y_i-p_i)^2\). Log loss is \(-n^{-1}\sum_i[y_i\log(p_i)+(1-y_i)\log(1-p_i)]\); probabilities are bounded between \(10^{-12}\) and \(1-10^{-12}\) for numerical scoring. Lower losses are better. AUC compares event and nonevent rankings with half credit for tied probabilities. AP sums precision over increments in recall after grouping equal probabilities. AP depends on event prevalence, so the two nested populations are not interchangeable benchmarks. We report probability loss, ranking, and calibration separately because improvement in one need not imply improvement in the others.
Counties are ordered by descending condition count, with county identifier breaking ties, and assigned to the currently least-loaded fold. Fold size, then county count, then fold number resolve assignment ties. This is a single deterministic partition, not repeated random cross-validation. The two populations receive their own size-balanced partition. Metrics pool all out-of-fold predictions within each population rather than averaging its five fold-specific AUC values. Appendix fold denominators show how many events actually support each held-out comparison.
Uncertainty uses 300 resamples per population of whole counties, repeating scaling and all held-out fits. All 600 resamples succeed. Original fold assignments, model set, and penalty remain fixed. Paired differences subtract the reference model on identical cases; negative Brier differences favor the added information. Percentile intervals characterize this resampling scheme. They exclude uncertainty from selecting the question, cohort, model set, and source snapshot. These data were already explored; this is not preregistration or external validation. The 300 draws provide finite Monte Carlo precision for the interval endpoints; their displayed digits should not be read as equally precise inferential information. No equivalence margin or minimum useful improvement was specified, and no multiple-comparison correction is applied. Interpretation emphasizes the matched Brier contrasts; additional metrics and secondary analyses are descriptive.
Each bootstrap draw samples the population’s counties with replacement, using the same number of county draws as observed counties. Every condition in a selected county receives its county’s sampling multiplicity as a frequency weight. All copies remain in that county’s original fold, so resampling cannot put a duplicate county into both training and testing. Weighted training means, sample standard deviations, model fits, and pooled scores are recomputed in each draw. Counties drawn zero times have no evaluation weight. The reported limits are the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of the 300 resulting metrics or paired differences, not standard errors calculated by treating 922 conditions as independent replicates. The stored seed is 20260908 in each population; this does not make the nested analyses independent.
Descriptive count-bin intervals use a separate 2,000-draw county resampling of observed event fractions, without fitting a model. A bin with no observed events has a degenerate empirical interval at zero; it does not establish a zero population risk. These intervals and the model-refit intervals answer different questions and should not be combined.
Fixed sensitivities restrict to exact overlap or follow-up manual version at least 9, or use penalties 0 and 4. A retrospective temporal assessment trains on follow-ups before 2023 and tests 2023 onward, with no shared physical plots. Realized interval is known at follow-up. Accordingly, these are conditional next-visit assessments, not validated fixed-horizon forecasts available at baseline. Count agreement and manual-version screening do not establish that every historical field procedure is identical; individual baseline regional editions were not all verified.


Linked sapling fates
A companion cohort follows live tagged baseline maple saplings on the expected successor plot before restricting follow-up species, status, or diameter. Comparable recorded death, live persistence below five inches, and live advancement to at least five inches are separated from frame inconsistency, species reidentification, and no-longer-sampled records. Fate eligibility is assessed separately from the new-entrant outcome: an ambiguous new arrival does not alone invalidate an existing tagged stem’s link. Annual diameter difference divides follow-up minus baseline diameter by elapsed years and is summarized only for comparable surviving maples. No mortality mechanism, treatment effect, or independent-stem sampling assumption is imposed.


Use of AI assistance
OpenAI Codex was used to assist with literature searching, analysis code development and checking, and manuscript revision. Computational checks do not constitute independent scientific review. Human authors retain responsibility for the data interpretation, references, and submitted content.

title: Ordinary seedling counts and recorded sugar maple sapling recruitment in Michigan northern hardwoods
text:
Discussion
Ordinary seedling counts contain information about recorded sapling entry in this selected Michigan sample. The count gradient and pooled probability-loss improvement argue against dismissing standard tallies as uninformative. However, discrimination is weaker within baseline detections, and its paired Brier improvement is uncertain. Abundant seedlings therefore indicate a higher chance of observing entry without establishing a secure advancing cohort.
The added maple-stage predictors produce only small, uncertain improvements over a strong count benchmark. They do not improve captured entrants at the tested equal capacity, and their survey-priority point gain over raw counts is not reproduced in the later-year comparison. These are substantive limits of the tested predictors and models, not reasons to continue adding variables until a preferred explanation appears. Uncertainty spanning zero is not proof of no effect, practical equivalence, or irrelevance under every model form.
In particular, existing sapling density and larger-tree basal area do not measure the height distribution of seedlings approaching the sapling boundary. Their uncertain incremental value therefore does not contradict evidence for height-resolved inventories (Harris et al. 2022). Our additive, transformed linear predictors also leave nonlinear responses and interactions untested. The results limit the specific benchmark models evaluated here, not all possible uses of stage structure.
The fate analysis explains why size-class absence and mortality must remain distinct. Surviving stems can move beyond the sapling boundary, while species reidentification and sampling corrections also alter apparent stage membership. Conversely, a new live sapling at one revisit does not measure all arrivals during the interval, adequate stocking, genetic origin, or subsequent survival to the canopy. Neither record-based endpoint supports a causal claim about browsing, competitors, or management.

Scope and limitations
The target is retained sampled conditions, not all Michigan forests. Baseline ecological selection, current-evaluation membership, accessible forest, remeasurement, comparable area, and unambiguous records restrict inclusion. The exclusion audit protects outcome interpretation but does not remove selection bias. County grouping addresses part of the dependence structure; it does not provide survey weights or independent experimental replication. The main scores give each condition interval equal weight, so plots contributing more than one condition receive more total evaluation weight.
Finite event support, estimated seedling tallies, varying sampled area and exposure duration, model-form choices, incomplete historical manual review, and one previously explored snapshot limit generalization. Resampling does not correct all of these limitations. Near-matching mean predicted and observed event fractions is not evidence of calibration everywhere, and the retrospective temporal split is not an untouched external test.
The two analysis populations are nested and do not provide independent replications. Observed entry combines growth into the defined diameter class, survival until remeasurement, and recording on a small sampled footprint. Zero recorded entry cannot distinguish slow growth from mortality or absence of suitable seedlings. Likewise, the tagged-stem fate sample does not follow the untagged baseline seedlings; it cannot decompose their failure to enter the sapling class. Unmeasured browsing, understory competition, and disturbance may influence these processes, but this analysis does not estimate their effects.


Implications and optional future work
The practical implication is to retain simple count-based benchmarks and state precisely what they predict. A management tool would additionally require a defined action, independently assessed survey need or treatment response, consequences of errors, and relevant external evaluation. No operational ranking or intervention rule is released.
Length structure is a plausible follow-on hypothesis motivated by earlier FIA work (Harris et al. 2022), not the unfulfilled central objective of this paper. A separate design specifies a matched count-versus-length comparison and evaluation safeguards. Regional inventory acquisition and field validation are deferred extensions. Wisconsin or Minnesota data are not required to complete the bounded Michigan results, and no regional outcome or height-model result is claimed. The earlier beech association concerned seedling-detection loss and remains in the supporting pilot; it is not recast as a recruitment mechanism.

title: Ordinary seedling counts and recorded sugar maple sapling recruitment in Michigan northern hardwoods
text:
Conclusion
Standard FIA seedling counts provide limited information about next-visit recorded sugar-maple sapling entry in selected Michigan northern hardwood conditions. Existing maple sapling density and established-maple basal area show no clear incremental improvement over the count benchmark under the specified comparisons. Linked tagged-stem accounting separately identifies recorded death, persistent live saplings, and surviving advancement beyond the sapling class. The core finding is an evidence-based boundary on what these common observations establish—not a claim of regeneration adequacy, biological failure, or validated management usefulness.

The RI comparison is a measurement audit on a smaller, partially overlapping sample, not a second validation of the main model. The observed tall-seedling contrast is not adjusted for ordinary counts, existing maple stages, sampled coverage, or temporal differences. Four later-year events cannot support the proposed added-length evaluation as if it were a well-powered held-out comparison.
The existing survey analysis tests fixed rankings and capacities against recorded outcomes. It does not measure travel time, treatment response, independent survey need, or the cost of a wrong decision. No deer-harvest, browsing, climate, or disturbance dataset has been joined to the core models. Those external-factor acquisition notes therefore supply neither an omitted adjusted effect nor additional validation for this paper.

A forest can contain many seedlings without those seedlings becoming the next generation of larger trees. This study compares repeated public USDA Forest Inventory and Analysis (FIA) observations in Michigan to ask what early maple counts tell us about new saplings recorded several years later.
Read the research report Explore the code
A forest condition is a mapped part of a plot with similar forest characteristics. Each paired observation links that area across two visits, typically seven years apart. Here, a sapling is a tree with a trunk at least 1 inch but less than 5 inches in diameter at breast height. It is not a mature canopy tree.

title: Canopy to Cohort
text:
Three findings to take away

More seedlings were a useful clue, not a guarantee
Conditions with higher starting counts more often had new maple saplings at the next visit. But even among the 280 conditions with more than 20 seedlings recorded initially, only 72 (25.7%) had a qualifying new sapling recorded later. Seedling abundance alone does not establish that the future forest is secure.



New saplings were recorded more often where the starting seedling count was higher. Bars show the percentage of sampled forest conditions with entry; vertical lines show county-resampling uncertainty. The zero-count group’s zero-width interval reflects no observed events, not proof that entry is impossible.




Adding more maple measurements did not clearly improve prediction
The study compared models on the same observations, testing each on counties excluded from its training data. Adding the abundance of existing maple saplings and larger maples produced small improvements in probability error, but the uncertainty included both improvement and worsening. These results do not yet show a dependable advantage over the simpler seedling-count model.
The models account for the area sampled and the time between visits. They are retrospective comparisons, not a validated tool for prescribing forest treatment.


Leaving the sapling size class does not always mean dying
A separate check followed 1,580 comparable, previously tagged maple saplings: 1,188 remained live saplings, 334 were recorded dead, and 58 remained alive after growing to at least 5 inches in trunk diameter. Keeping these outcomes separate prevents healthy growth from being mistaken for loss.

title: Canopy to Cohort
section: What this means for forest assessment
text:
What this means for forest assessment
Seedling counts are worth measuring, but they are one part of the picture. Repeated visits help distinguish new sapling entry, continued survival, growth into a larger size class, and recorded death.
No new sapling recorded does not by itself mean regeneration has failed. The inventory samples small areas, seedlings are not individually tagged, and some entrants may die or grow beyond the studied size class between visits. These are unweighted results for the study sample, not statewide rates.

title: Canopy to Cohort
text:
How the question developed
The earlier detection study examined whether seedlings were recorded at one visit and not at the next. That is a different question from whether young trees entered the sapling class. The new study audits repeated FIA visits and newly recorded stems to examine that transition directly. It does not claim to follow individual seedlings into individual saplings.
The research direction explains this progression. The full report places the analysis alongside existing FIA research and provides the statistical comparisons, uncertainty, and limitations.

title: Canopy to Cohort
text:
What remains to be tested
Two possible extensions are documented separately from the completed findings:

Seedling length: a smaller measurement audit suggests a reason to test whether taller seedlings add information beyond counts. Only 14 conditions in that subset had new saplings, so no added-length prediction claim is made. See the measurement audit and follow-up study design.
Deer and browsing: public sources have been assessed, but a suitable geographic match and exposure measure remain unresolved. No deer effect has been estimated in this study. See the source-feasibility assessment.

A survey-priority comparison also tests simple rules against the models. It does not establish fieldwork benefit or a treatment recommendation.

title: Canopy to Cohort
text:
Abstract
This exploratory study links 932 repeated Michigan Forest Inventory and Analysis (FIA) forest conditions with established sugar maple at baseline, accessible sampling at both visits, one-to-one mapping, and comparable microplot footprints. Visits were separated by 5.4–8.1 years. Of 677 baseline seedling detections, 75 became non-detections. County-held-out validation of a seven-slope logistic model gave Brier 0.08151 and AUC 0.856, compared with 0.08253 and 0.845 for starting abundance, coverage, and interval alone. The added predictive improvement is small and uncertain under a paired county bootstrap conditional on existing fitted folds. Sixty of 75 losses began with no more than five tallied seedlings. Among 255 baseline non-detections, 59 became detections; a four-slope appearance model had weak held-out discrimination (AUC 0.566). Neither endpoint measures individual survival or sapling recruitment. The pilot is retained as measurement evidence; the revised primary goal evaluates recruitment and linked sapling fates rather than promoting a detection-risk tool.

title: Canopy to Cohort
text:
1 Why the research direction changed
The first project release asked which size classes occurred together at one visit. That work produced an important measurement result: combining 1–4.9-inch saplings with trees at least 5 inches DBH made “maple abundance” look more informative than established-tree abundance alone. Once FIA size classes were separated, sapling presence—not additional established-maple basal area—carried most of the same-visit association.
Repeated conditions improved time ordering, but the detection pilot still leaves the central ecological question unanswered: do observed seedlings lead to advancing regeneration? Presence can persist without advancement, while disappearance from a size class can include growth into a larger class. The current direction review therefore changes the primary endpoint, not merely the model’s complexity.
Michigan studies report abundant small seedlings alongside limited larger regeneration (Henry et al. 2021), and show that small-diameter sugar maples can be old, suppressed stems (Henry and Walters 2023). Regional FIA studies distinguish favorable small-seedling composition from low sugar-maple sapling abundance (Harris et al. 2026b). Browse relationships vary by size class (Harris et al. 2025). The Canadian beech association is a candidate hypothesis, with geography, size-class definitions, and relative-abundance measures limiting transfer (Gauthier 2025).
Crucially, prior research already predicts FIA sapling recruitment and compares ordinary seedling counts with six height classes (Harris et al. 2022); advance-regeneration prediction after disturbance is also established (Harris et al. 2026a). A useful contribution here must be a Michigan evaluation of indicator performance and limitations, not a claim that longitudinal FIA forecasting is novel.

title: Canopy to Cohort
text:
2 Questions addressed by this pilot
The pilot’s primary question was:

Among Michigan northern-hardwood conditions with established sugar maple and seedlings detected at baseline, which baseline characteristics predict no seedling detection at the next FIA measurement?

Four secondary questions keep the interpretation honest:

How often do the four detection transitions—persistent non-detection, appearance, loss, and persistence—occur?
Does American beech sapling basal area add information beyond starting seedling density and general stand structure?
Does the risk signal survive when whole counties are withheld during model fitting?
Among baseline non-detections, can a lean model forecast later detection appearance?

The estimand is a repeated observation probability. It is not individual seedling survival, recruitment into the sapling class, or a causal effect of competition or management.

3 Data and cohort

3.1 FIA source and analytical grain
The analysis uses the Michigan SQLite release from the U.S. Forest Service FIA DataMart (U.S. Forest Service 2026) and pins current evaluation “MICHIGAN 2025: 2019-2025: CURRENT AREA, CURRENT VOLUME” (EVALID 262501; inventory window 2019–2025). Sugar maple resolves from REF_SPECIES to Acer saccharum (SPCD 318), American beech to Fagus grandifolia (SPCD 531), and the baseline northern-hardwood cohort to active forest-type group 800 codes (Burrill et al. 2025).
The unit is one linked pair of FIA plot conditions. Control numbers are relational identifiers, not coordinates. Exact FIA plot locations are neither used nor inferred; county identifiers are retained only for grouped validation.


3.2 Following the same microplot footprint
SUBP_COND_CHNG_MTRX supplies the authoritative condition linkage. Because seedlings are sampled on microplots, the extraction uses SUBPTYP = 2. Rows are first aggregated to each baseline–follow-up condition pair:
\[
Overlap_{bc} = \frac{1}{4}\sum_{s=1}^{4} SUBPTYP\_PROP\_CHNG_{bcs}.
\]
Pair degrees are computed before ecological filters. The primary cohort retains only bidirectional one-to-one links, then requires the overlap divided by both baseline and follow-up MICRPROP_UNADJ to be at least 0.90. Small conditions are therefore not rejected merely because their absolute area share is below 0.90. Among strict links, the minimum observed relative overlap was 0.991.
Baseline eligibility requires a sampled accessible-forest condition in forest-type group 800, positive microplot coverage, and at least one live sugar-maple TREE record with DBH ≥5 inches. Follow-up must be sampled accessible forest with positive microplot coverage. It is not required to remain in group 800 because follow-up classification is post-baseline; 98.2% nevertheless remained in that group.

6 Discussion


What the evidence supports

Seedling detection is usually persistent, but roughly one in nine baseline detections became a zero tally at the next visit.
Low starting seedling tallies are strongly associated with later zero tallies.
Detection opportunity must remain explicit when interpreting these transitions.
The stand variables add little prediction beyond abundance and observation; beech remains an exploratory association.
County-held-out detection ranking is not evidence of recruitment prediction or management value.
Detection appearance occurred in nearly one quarter of baseline non-detections, but the tested compact model did not forecast it reliably.



What it does not establish

That the original seedlings died or that sugar maple became locally extinct.
That American beech caused the change rather than marking browsing, soils, disturbance history, or other site conditions.
Which management treatment would prevent loss.
Statewide or county prevalence under the formal FIA survey design.
Performance in another state, inventory cycle, or independent field study.
That the appearance model can identify sites likely to gain seedlings.



The earlier recommendation to use this model for field triage was premature. A triage study would need a regeneration-relevant outcome, a stated survey objective and capacity, and evidence of improvement over a simple abundance rule. The present pilot supplies none of those operational validations. Its useful contribution is to expose the distinction between repeat detection and advancing regeneration.
The beech signal could reflect competitive pressure, deer selectivity, site fertility, sprouting history, or unmeasured management. It is one hypothesis among several, not a prescription or sufficient reason to organize the next study around beech.

title: Canopy to Cohort
text:
7 Limitations

Detection, not tracked survival. FIA seedlings are tally records, not tagged individuals. A transition to zero can reflect mortality, growth out of the size class, spatial turnover, phenology, or imperfect detection.
Conditioning and repeated counts. The loss model begins with positive baseline tallies and uses their density as its strongest predictor. Low positive counts are mechanically more likely to become zero under repeated sampling, so this coefficient can reflect regression to the mean or count variability even when latent abundance is stable.
Observation footprint. Although all primary pairs share at least 90% of both condition footprints—and in practice at least 99.1%—smaller microplot condition shares still provide fewer opportunities to encounter seedlings.
Strict-pair selection. Split, merged, inaccessible, and nonforest follow-ups are excluded from the primary biological outcome. Nine otherwise eligible strict baseline conditions lacked a comparable follow-up.
Two observations. One interval identifies a transition but not a trajectory, lag structure, or recruitment rate.
Prognostic coefficients. Baseline associations do not identify causal effects. Inter-visit treatment was deliberately excluded from the primary model because timing and confounding by indication are inadequate for causal inference.
Unmeasured mechanisms. Browse, detailed seedling height, soils, invasive plants, and understory vegetation are available only for small nested FIA subsets.
Internal validation. County-held-out validation tests geographic transport within Michigan, not external generalization. The reassessment reuses these folds; its bootstrap is conditional on fitted predictions. This is exploratory reanalysis, not untouched confirmation.
Weak gain model. The secondary appearance model has low discrimination and shrinkage-prone calibration. Appearance may depend on unmeasured seed production, microsites, browse, disturbance timing, or count variation; it is not a usable site-level gain forecast.
Survey estimand. TPA_UNADJ and condition proportions support within-plot density construction; they are not statewide survey weights. Formal prevalence requires FIA population-estimation procedures (Bechtold and Patterson 2005).

The pipeline records 85 hashed source artifacts, a pinned evaluation, condition-link audits, frame-specific basal-area validation, cohort flow, scaling constants, model support, county-cluster inference, nested model comparisons, fold assignments, held-out predictions for both conditional outcomes, and tests. The mapping audit found zero broken condition references and zero disagreements between matrix predecessor links and PLOT.PREV_PLT_CN.

The direction-audit target runs the benchmark and recruitment-feasibility audits in scripts 11 and 12. Raw, interim, and record-level processed FIA data remain excluded from version control; aggregate evidence and figures contain no plot coordinates.

9 Next research step
The recruitment study now tests whether ordinary seedling and sapling observations anticipate new sapling recruitment. Its audited cohort contains 922 intervals, 169 new live saplings in 100 conditions, and a companion linked-stem fate analysis. The original 171-stem feasibility screen and 2,308 historical candidate intervals are retained in the direction audit; they are not the final recruitment model population. See the current goals for what is implemented and what remains unresolved.
First validate ingrowth codes, sampling-frame continuity, species corrections, and sampled zero-tree visits. Then compare a small sequence of observation, abundance, and stage-structure models using grouped validation and a retrospective temporal check. Report surviving growth, death, and identity changes separately. RI height classes are a conditional extension if repeated Michigan support proves adequate; any browse predictor needs a circularity check. Negative or imprecise incremental results are valid outcomes of this study.

title: Regeneration length classes and measurement feasibility
text:
The Michigan regeneration-indicator (RI) records support a descriptive measurement study, but not a strong new forecasting claim. The baseline sampling and record checks retain 90 condition intervals on 87 physical plots, with 14 recruit-bearing conditions. The appropriate next scientific question is whether seedling length distribution adds information beyond ordinary counts on the same sampled area, not whether another stand variable can improve a headline metric.
Taller seedlings provide a plausible lead. Among 44 conditions with RI maple seedlings at least five feet long, 13 had recorded new saplings at follow-up; among 46 without such seedlings, 1 did. This is a retrospective association in an already explored sample. It is not a held-out comparison with seedling abundance, proof of individual survival, or a management threshold.
The information constraint remains decisive: the existing later-year split would provide 10 development events and 4 assessment events. No height-class model is fitted. The current contribution is a reconciled measurement audit and a more specific testable hypothesis; evidence for an operational survey tool remains absent.

title: Regeneration length classes and measurement feasibility
text:
Endpoint and population
The source population is the 922 eligible intervals from the recruitment study, not all Michigan forest conditions. The outcome remains a new live sugar-maple sapling tally at follow-up, using the existing species, diameter, reconciliation, predecessor, and shared-sampling checks. No eligibility rule is relaxed to obtain more RI records or events.
Baseline RI is a potential predictor. Follow-up RI is a different measurement and is not needed to establish baseline length structure when the follow-up TREE endpoint is otherwise valid. Requiring RI at both visits would answer a narrower question and could discard valid baseline observations. Neither condition intervals nor sampled microplots are whole management stands, and these results are not statewide, survey-weighted population estimates.

title: Regeneration length classes and measurement feasibility
text:
Sampling and protocol definitions
The database dictionary retires REGEN_SUBP_STATUS_CD from inventory year 2015 and identifies REGEN_MICR_STATUS_CD as the status field populated across years. Code 1 identifies sampled RI on accessible forest; code 2 is sampled but without accessible forest on the microplot. Codes 3-5 are nonsampled and code 9 is historically ambiguous. A blank retired field is therefore not a reason to reject an otherwise valid code-1 forest sample. Conversely, code 2 cannot verify RI coverage of a positive forest-condition area. (Burrill et al. 2025, sec. 6.2.10 and 6.2.22)
The baseline screen requires RI plot presence, code-1 coverage of every contributing condition-microplot slice, consistent subplot identifiers, compatible core sampling, and a reconstructed condition area matching the existing microplot proportion. RI seedling records must have valid condition and subplot-condition foreign keys, species/source/length codes, and counts. Duplicate keys stop the calculation; invalid records make the affected plot’s RI measurements unavailable. Missing species tallies are not zero-filled until the measurement frame passes.
The inspected annual supplements specify a May-September RI window and established seedlings at least two inches long, below one inch DBH. Length is measured along the seedling from base to terminal bud, not necessarily vertical height. Counts above five may be estimated. Stump sprouts and suckers from one origin are not independent stems; only the tallest qualifying stump sprout is tallied. These details limit biological interpretations of the count totals. (U.S. Forest Service 2016, sec. 6.0 and 6.4; U.S. Forest Service 2018, 18–22)

Historical coverage and date limitations
The full relevant sections of the 2016, 2017, and 2018 annual supplements were inspected. These years cover 37 available baseline intervals with four events. These qualifications are retained in the protocol note.
PLOT.MANUAL is not treated as a precise P2+ supplement edition: for example, baseline records store 7.0 while the available annual supplements include 7.1 and 7.2. Year-specific documentary coverage is recorded separately. Plot measurement dates provide a plausibility screen, not proof of the exact RI measurement day or leaf condition; the RI tables expose no separate field date.

title: Regeneration length classes and measurement feasibility
text:
Forecasting feasibility and next decision
A development/assessment split following the existing calendar boundary has 53 development intervals with ten events and 37 later intervals with four events, with no shared physical plots across the split. One missed assessment event would change observed event recall by 25 percentage points. These already explored outcomes are not an untouched validation set even if their length predictors were previously unused.
As a precision illustration only, even a hypothetical rule finding all 14 event plots would have an exact two-sided binomial 95% lower recall bound of 76.8% under independent-event sampling. This is not the observed rule’s recall, a clustered confidence interval, or a sample-size justification. Geographic dependence and a held-out sample would further constrain what can be learned.
The evidence supports retaining length structure as the next measurement hypothesis. It does not support a six-class fitted forecasting model or an operational score from this subset. A useful next study would fix a single supportable length representation, retain ordinary counts and sampling area as comparators on identical cases, and evaluate the paired gain in a separate, adequately supported inventory sample. A meaningful gain, forecasting horizon, decision target, action unit, and measurement cost must be specified first.
Within the existing Michigan snapshot, the baseline measurement milestone is complete with the historical-access qualifications above. The defensible contribution is the distinction between seedling abundance, length structure, and recorded sapling entry, together with explicit limits on usefulness. Acquiring other inventories or coordinating field work requires a separate scope decision; neither has occurred. The survey validation plan records these gates.
The subsequent count-versus-length design fixes a one-term comparison and planning scenarios. Its outcome-free historical opportunity screen finds only six physical plots beyond the current recruitment cohort among positive-seedling opportunities, before full eligibility checks. It does not establish a new independent Michigan test sample.

title: Research direction and goals
text:
The bounded Michigan core research is complete as of September 9, 2026. The revised paper answers the count-information, incremental-stage, and linked-fate questions. Regional data acquisition and length-model validation are deferred optional extensions, not prerequisites for completing this paper. The results do not justify another pivot merely because added-model improvements are small or uncertain.
Change the primary question to whether observed sugar-maple regeneration leads to recorded recruitment into the sapling size class. Retain the existing seedling-detection analysis as an exploratory measurement study. Its numerical results remain useful, but the earlier claim that it establishes a field-triage tool is withdrawn.
The project’s goal is:

Determine how well ordinary FIA seedling and sapling observations anticipate new sugar-maple sapling recruitment in Michigan northern hardwoods, measure what additional stand information contributes, and distinguish recruitment, survival, growth, and observation changes.

The intended contribution is a transparent Michigan evaluation of regeneration indicators. Its novelty must come from a useful comparison and credible validation. Linking repeated FIA visits or fitting a prediction model is already established in the literature.
The direction decision was made on September 7. The first recruitment analysis was implemented on September 8; its results are summarized below and in the recruitment report. The existing data have been explored; this is not a preregistration or external validation.
